reason: This was the line I expected to break, because the sentence circulates in several smoothed renderings (Gladwin's 'Riches are for the comfort of life, and not life for the sake of hoarding riches', and a web answer that offered me 'Property is for the comfort of life, not for the accumulation of wealth'). It survives. I downloaded the full OCR of the Internet Archive scan the evidence names (gulistanorrosega00sadiuoft) and found the passage set exactly as proposed: '205 / CHAPTER VIII. / ON THE DUTIES OF SOCIETY. / Maxim I. / Riches are for the sake of making life comfortable, not life for the sake of amassing riches. I asked a wise man, “Who is fortunate and who unfortunate?” He replied, “The fortunate is he who sowed and reaped; the unfortunate he who died and abandoned.”' Word for word, including 'making life comfortable' and 'amassing', which is what the smoothed versions lose. Locator confirmed: the bare 205 heads the chapter opening and the next page carries the running head '206 GULISTAN; OR, ROSE GARDEN.', with 'CHAPTER VIII. MAXIM VII. 207' after it, so Maxim I stands on p. 205. Edition confirmed from the same scan's title page: Trubner's Oriental Series, 'THE GULISTAN; OR, ROSE-GARDEN, OF SHEKH MUSLIHU'D-DIN SADI OF SHIRAZ', translated by Edward B. Eastwick, SECOND EDITION, London, Trubner and Co., 1880. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Saadi at 0 of 3, not banned. Thirteenth century and Persian, so it earns its place on century and country. Not scripture: the Gulistan is a literary didactic work and the quoted maxim carries no religious matter. Publishable.
